tone_statements.citation: Kumar, Pramod. 2012. Descriptive and typological study of Jarawa. PhD dissertation, Jawaharlal Nehru University, New Delhi. xv+342 pp.
tone_statements.quote: In a discussion of typological features of the phonology of a language, the following points are generally discussed: i) Whether the language is tonal or non-tonal. ii) Which kind of vowel system has been adopted? iii) Which kind of distinction is present at consonantal level? iv) What is the syllabic structure? v) What kinds of syllabic structure are common in this language at word level? Jarawa is a non-tonal language. It employs a seven-vowel system with a three- way distinction in height and a two-way distinction in the horizontal position of the raised part of the tongue. Thus, this language has /i/, /e/, /a/, /o/, /u/, /ə/ and /ᵼ/. This seven-vowel system also has contrast in length.
tone_statements.locator: p. 199, Chapter 5, section 5.2 'Phonological typology of Jarawa'

sources.citation: Mekrazi, Djilali. 2025. La langue Jarawa. Self-published PDF (archive.org 'la-langue-jarawa').

sources.citation: Blevins, Juliette. 2007. A long lost sister of Proto-Austronesian? Proto-Ongan, mother of Jarawa and Onge of the Andaman Islands. Oceanic Linguistics 46(1): 154-198 (author-posted PDF via the Internet Archive of email.eva.mpg.de/~blevins/pdf/).
sources.note: Sec. 2.1 'Synchronic phonology' (pp. 160-162) gives Jarawa/Onge inventories, max CVC syllable, bimoraic minimal content word, four processes after Abbi 2006 -- no stress placement. Sec. 2.2 presupposes word stress without locating it: 'Jarawa e is often reduced to [schwa] in unstressed syllables' (p. 164); 'Reduction of the nonround nonhigh vowels *e and *a to schwa in unstressed syllables is variable' (p. 164); cognate-set notes refer to 'where u is stressed.. where final i is stressed' (p. 167). No rule for where stress falls.

Ch. 2 'Phonetics and Phonology' (pp. 36-72) is explicitly segmental ('with focus on segmental phonology', p. 36): inventory, contrasts, distribution, syllable structure V/CV/VC/CVC (2.4, p. 65), syllabification (2.5), word structure (2.6), morphophonemics (2.7). No suprasegmental/stress/accent/tone section; the string 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the thesis text.

tone.says: States outright that Jarawa is a non-tonal language (sec. 5.2 'Phonological typology of Jarawa', p. 199), as the first of five typological parameters; the phonology chapter (ch. 2, pp. 36-72) has no suprasegmental section and the thesis nowhere discusses pitch, stress or intonation.
